conventions.topics: same topic tags as the ASA 101 Study Kit: parts, sail, trim, rules, lights, aton, nav, knots, safety, weather, dock
conventions.drills: drill ids from drill-briefings.json, or Any for questions that fit any sail (rules, weather, safety)
conventions.answer: zero-based index into options; shuffle options at run time and keep the answer with its text
conventions.why: one line shown after the player answers
conventions.source: written for the sim; none duplicates a question in the ASA 101 Study Kit artifact

questions.q: Before leaving Rush Creek on a July afternoon, which check matters most for the next few hours?
options: The radar and forecast for thunderstorms
questions.why: Summer storms build fast over North Texas in the afternoon; Ray Hubbard has no tides.

questions.q: Tied up with the bow pointing into the wind, which sail do you usually hoist first?
options: Neither until you are clear of the marina
questions.why: Head to wind, the main luffs harmlessly along the centreline; the jib adds power you do not need yet.

questions.q: While you hoist the mainsail, the mainsheet should be:
options: Eased so the sail can luff freely
questions.why: A loose sheet lets the sail luff head to wind instead of filling and pushing the boat around.

questions.q: The wind is pinning your boat against the dock. What is the safer plan?
options: Trim both sails in tight before casting off
Hoist the jib and push off hard
Cast off all lines and wait for the boat to drift clear
Walk the boat to a spot where it can point into the wind, or use the motor
questions.why: Sailing off a leeward dock is very hard; move the boat or use the engine instead.

questions.q: Why do you want a little speed soon after leaving the dock?
options: It keeps the boat from heeling
Speed keeps the sails from luffing
The keel only works above 3 knots
The rudder only steers with water flowing past it
questions.why: With no flow over the rudder the boat will not turn where you push the tiller.

questions.q: When should the fenders come aboard after leaving the dock?
options: Once you are clear of the dock and other boats
As soon as the main is up
questions.why: They protect the hull while you leave; after that they just drag and look sloppy.

questions.q: Once you are clear of the marina, the dock lines should be:
options: Left trailing to slow the boat
Coiled and stowed so nothing trails over the side
questions.why: A trailing line can foul the rudder or outboard, and loose lines underfoot trip the crew.

questions.q: Ray Hubbard has no tides. What mostly changes the depth near the docks?
options: The lake level, which rises after rain and falls in drought
questions.why: Reservoir levels move with rainfall, drought and water use, so check the lake level before you go.

questions.q: Many inflatable life jackets count toward the Coast Guard requirement only when they are:
questions.why: Check the label: many inflatables count only when worn, and all need their gas cylinder armed and serviced.

questions.q: Which tells you the wind direction at the dock most reliably?
options: The direction the boat in the next slip is facing
The direction of the waves from passing powerboats
Flags, ripples on the water and the masthead fly together
questions.why: Use several signs; wakes and moored boats can mislead you.

questions.q: Before casting off, the skipper should brief the crew on:
options: Who handles which line and where to sit
questions.why: A short briefing turns a scramble into a calm departure.

questions.q: The windward mark is straight upwind. How do you get there?
options: Sail a zigzag of close-hauled legs, tacking between them
Sail straight at it with the sails tight
questions.why: A sailboat cannot sail into the no-go zone, so it beats upwind in a series of tacks.

questions.q: Close-hauled, both jib telltales are streaming and you want to point higher. You should:
options: Head up until the windward telltale starts to lift, then bear away a touch
Trim the jib until both telltales droop
questions.why: The windward telltale lifting is the sign you have reached the edge of the no-go zone.

questions.q: To head up, you push the tiller toward:
questions.why: Tiller toward the sail turns the bow toward the wind.

questions.q: From close-hauled you bear away to a beam reach with the sails eased correctly. The boat usually:
questions.why: Off the wind the sail force points more forward, so the boat stands up and accelerates.

questions.q: For most keelboats without a spinnaker, the fastest point of sail is about:
questions.why: On a beam reach the sails drive well and the apparent wind stays strong.

questions.q: To avoid stopping in irons during a tack, you should:
options: Have good speed first and turn steadily through the wind
questions.why: Momentum carries the bow through head to wind; a slow turn loses it.

questions.q: What does the helmsman's call "Helm's a-lee" tell the crew?
options: There is a boat to leeward
The tiller is over and the boat is turning through the wind
The boat is about to jibe
questions.why: It is the moment the turn starts; the crew release the old jib sheet as the jib luffs.

questions.q: Feathering means:
options: Easing the jib all the way
Steering slightly closer to the wind in a puff so the sails luff a little and the boat heels less
questions.why: It is a quick way to depower upwind without touching the sheets.

questions.q: Telltales on the leech of the mainsail help you set the:
questions.why: If the leech telltales curl behind the sail, the main is over-trimmed: ease the mainsheet.

questions.q: At the wing mark you turn from one reach to the other with the wind passing behind the boat. That maneuver is a:
questions.why: When the stern turns through the wind it is a jibe.

questions.q: The call that starts the turn in a jibe is:
questions.why: "Prepare to jibe", "Ready", then "Jibe-ho" as the helm turns.

questions.q: At the wing mark you head up from a broad reach to a close reach. The sheets should be:
questions.why: The closer you sail to the wind, the more the sails need to be trimmed in.

questions.q: A south wind on Lake Ray Hubbard means the windward mark is laid:
questions.why: Winds are named for where they come from, and the windward mark goes upwind.

questions.q: The no-go zone for a boat like the J/22 is roughly:
options: Within about 45 degrees either side of the wind
questions.why: Closer than about 45 degrees, the sails cannot fill and the boat stops.

questions.q: On a run with the wind directly behind, the mainsail should be:
options: Eased nearly at right angles to the boat
questions.why: Downwind the sail works by blocking the wind, so it goes all the way out.

questions.q: Wing-on-wing means:
options: Main on one side and jib on the other, running downwind
Both sails on the same side
Two boats sailing side by side
questions.why: Holding the jib out on the opposite side catches more wind on a run.

questions.q: When a boat is hove to, the jib is:
options: Backed, held on the windward side
Trimmed normally on the leeward side
questions.why: The backed jib pushes the bow away from the wind.

questions.q: When hove to, the tiller is held or lashed:
questions.why: With the tiller to leeward the rudder tries to turn the bow up, balancing the backed jib.

questions.q: When hove to, the mainsail is:
questions.why: It only needs a little drive to balance the jib.

questions.q: The simplest way to back the jib to heave to is:
options: Tack without releasing the jib sheet
Lower the jib and raise it on the other side
Ease the jib all the way out
questions.why: The jib stays on the old side and fills backward once the bow is through.

questions.q: A boat that is properly hove to:
options: Creeps forward slowly and drifts to leeward
questions.why: Expect about a knot of slow forward and sideways drift.

questions.q: Which is a good reason to heave to?
options: To tie in a reef as a storm approaches
questions.why: Heaving to stops the boat so you can reef, rest, eat or sort out a problem.

questions.q: Before heaving to, check that you have open water:
questions.why: You drift downwind while hove to, so you need room to leeward.

questions.q: Why does a boat stay put when hove to?
options: The backed jib and the rudder push the bow in opposite directions and balance
The keel locks it in place
The mainsail is acting as a brake
questions.why: The forces cancel, leaving a slow drift.

questions.q: To get going again from hove to, you:
options: Release the backed jib, trim it on the leeward side and straighten the tiller
Push the tiller further to leeward
questions.why: Free the jib to the leeward side and steer off; the boat sails away.

questions.q: In the figure-eight recovery, after the shout and the flotation, you sail away on a:
questions.why: A beam reach is easy to sail and easy to reverse.

questions.q: About how far do you sail away before turning back in a figure-eight?
options: Until you lose sight of them
A few boat lengths, about four or five
questions.why: Far enough to set up a slow approach, close enough to keep them in sight.

questions.q: Why tack rather than jibe to turn back in a figure-eight?
options: Jibing loses sight of the person
Tacking is faster in all winds
A tack is more controlled; a hurried jibe can swing the boom violently
questions.why: In an emergency you want the calm maneuver.

questions.q: After tacking in the figure-eight, you bear away to a broad reach so that you end up:
options: A little downwind of the person
questions.why: From downwind you can turn up onto a close reach for the final approach.

questions.q: Your final approach to the person is too fast. The best fix is to:
options: Steer straight at them and hope
Ease the sheets more, and if still too fast, sail past and set up again
questions.why: Never rush a pick-up; another lap is safer than hitting the person.

questions.q: Right after shouting "Crew overboard!", someone should throw:
options: A throwable flotation device, like a cushion or ring
questions.why: It gives them something to hold and marks where they are.

questions.q: Once alongside the person in the water, the first thing to do is:
options: Lift them aboard by the arms immediately
Get a line on them so they are attached to the boat
questions.why: Once they are secured you can work out how to get them aboard without losing them.

questions.q: For the final few metres of a crew-overboard pick-up, you turn into the wind so that:
options: The person drifts away from the boat
The headwind and luffing sails slow the boat to a stop
The jib fills and adds speed
You can only pick them up on the starboard side
questions.why: Head to wind the sails stop driving; you can bring them aboard on port or starboard.

questions.q: Many GPS units and VHF radios have an MOB button. Pressing it:
options: Marks the position where the person went in
questions.why: It records the spot so you can steer back to it if you lose sight of them.

questions.q: Why is approaching the person on a run a bad idea?
options: You cannot slow down by luffing the sails downwind
questions.why: Downwind the sails keep pulling even when eased.

questions.q: In cold water, the first danger to a person who falls in is:
options: Cold shock: gasping and loss of breath control
questions.why: Cold shock hits in the first minute; that is why a life jacket matters so much.

questions.q: A person in the water drifts:
options: Slowly downwind, more slowly than a drifting sailboat
questions.why: The person drifts slowly; your boat, with sails and topsides, drifts faster.

questions.q: The quick-stop method begins by:
options: Heading up into the wind immediately
Sailing away on a beam reach
questions.why: Turning into the wind stops the boat right away, close to the person.

questions.q: During the quick-stop, the jib is:
options: Released and trimmed on the new side
Left backed to help the bow come around
questions.why: The backed jib pushes the bow around so you can keep circling.

questions.q: A key advantage of the quick-stop over the figure-eight is that:
options: It keeps the boat close to the person the whole time
It can only be done with a large crew
questions.why: You never get far away, which matters most when you are short-handed.

questions.q: In the quick-stop you keep turning after the tack until you are:
options: Downwind of the person, ready to come up on a close reach
Pointing straight at them on a run
questions.why: From downwind, a close-reach approach lets you luff to stop.

questions.q: You and one friend are sailing and your friend falls in. Which method suits a crew of one best?
options: Quick-stop, because it stays close and needs little sail handling
questions.why: The quick-stop is mostly steering, which one person can manage.

questions.q: The first thing to decide when planning a docking approach is:
options: The wind direction relative to the dock
questions.why: Everything else, from heading to where you luff, follows from the wind.

questions.q: Why is approaching a dock on a run a bad idea?
options: You cannot slow down by luffing; the sails keep pulling
questions.why: You need to finish heading close to the wind so that easing the sheets takes the power off.

questions.q: Why do you start luffing well before the dock in a keelboat?
options: It is required by the rules
The sails take a minute to luff
Its weight keeps it moving a long way
questions.why: A J/22 weighs over 800 kg and glides a long way after the sails stop driving.

questions.q: The ideal speed when you reach the dock is:
options: Full speed so you can steer
Barely moving, slower than a walk
questions.why: Arrive slowly enough that a crew member can step off and stop the boat with a line.

questions.q: Your approach is clearly going wrong 20 metres out. The best choice is to:
options: Keep going and fend off hard
Abort early: turn away and go around
questions.why: A second approach costs a minute; a crash costs a lot more.

questions.q: Fenders should be put out:
options: On both sides only in strong wind
Before you enter the marina, on the side you will dock
questions.why: Set them early, at the height where the hull meets the dock.

questions.q: A crew member getting off at the dock should:
options: Jump while the boat is still well off
Step off with a line once the boat is close and slow
Hold the boat off with a leg
questions.why: Step, don't jump, and take a line so the boat can be stopped.

questions.q: The usual way to make a dock line fast to a cleat is a:
questions.why: A turn around the base, a figure-eight over the horns, and a locking hitch.

questions.q: Head to wind after tying up, the usual order to lower the sails is:
questions.why: The jib comes down first so the main keeps the bow head to wind.

questions.q: You run aground softly in mud near a point on the lake. A good first try is to:
options: Ease the sails, turn back the way you came, and heel the boat with crew weight
Trim in hard and sail forward
questions.why: Heeling lifts the keel a little, and the way you came in is known to be deep enough.

questions.q: With the wind blowing you off the dock, the danger is that:
options: The boat is pinned against the dock
The boat drifts away before the lines are on
questions.why: Get the windward lines on quickly, or the boat blows away from the crew on the dock.

questions.q: You are on port tack. A Catalina 22 on starboard tack is crossing ahead of you from the right. The best way to keep clear is usually to:
options: Bear away early to pass behind her
questions.why: As give-way boat, act early and obviously; passing astern is the safe choice.

questions.q: Under the Navigation Rules, a personal watercraft (jet ski) is:
questions.why: Anything propelled by machinery is a power-driven vessel.

questions.q: A bass boat is trolling a single fishing line. Under the rules, is it a vessel "engaged in fishing"?
options: No, trolling lines do not restrict its maneuverability
questions.why: Only gear that restricts maneuverability, like nets or trawls, counts.

questions.q: You are sailing with the outboard running in gear. A sailboat under sail alone crosses from your left. Who gives way?
options: You, because you count as power-driven
questions.why: With the engine propelling you, you are a power-driven vessel and give way to a sailing vessel.

questions.q: The give-way vessel is clearly not acting and a collision can no longer be avoided by her alone. The stand-on vessel must:
options: Sound one long blast and continue
Hold course and speed no matter what
Take whatever action best avoids the collision
questions.why: Rule 17: when the give-way vessel's action alone cannot prevent a collision, the stand-on vessel must act too.

questions.q: A faster boat overtakes you on the same tack and passes to leeward of you. Who must keep clear?
options: You, because you are to windward
questions.why: The overtaking rule comes first and overrides the windward-leeward rule.

questions.q: Even when you are the stand-on vessel, the rules expect you to:
options: Sound five blasts at every boat
Use good seamanship and keep a proper lookout
questions.why: Responsibility and lookout rules apply to everyone, all the time.

questions.q: A powerboat is approaching on a steady bearing and closing, and the driver does not seem to see you. Your first step is to:
options: Ignore it; sail has right of way
Watch closely and be ready to act, signalling if you can
questions.why: A steady bearing means collision risk; never count on the other driver knowing the rules.

questions.q: Which vessel should a small sailboat keep clear of?
options: A powerboat crossing from your starboard side
A jet ski crossing from your port side
questions.why: An anchored vessel cannot get out of the way, so everyone keeps clear of it.

questions.q: A big powerboat wake is coming toward you. The best way to meet it is to:
options: Turn the bow to meet it at an angle and hold on
questions.why: Taking a wake at an angle softens the roll and keeps the boat dry.

questions.q: Rule 5 requires every vessel to keep a proper lookout:
options: By sight and hearing at all times
questions.why: Most collisions start with nobody looking.

questions.q: Before a thunderstorm's rain reaches you, you can expect:
options: A sudden strong, gusty wind shift from the gust front
questions.why: Outflow from the storm often arrives minutes before the rain.

questions.q: A thunderstorm rule of thumb says that if the time between a lightning flash and its thunder is under 30 seconds, you should:
options: Seek shelter, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back out
Keep sailing; it's still far off
Raise the jib to get home faster
questions.why: This is the 30-30 rule.

questions.q: A fall cold front passing over North Texas usually brings:
options: A wind shift to the south and heat
A wind shift to the north with gusts and cooler air
questions.why: Fronts can swing the wind north quickly and strongly; reef early.

questions.q: In North Texas, the National Weather Service warning for strong winds on area lakes is called a:
questions.why: Inland offices issue Lake Wind Advisories; small craft advisories are for coastal waters.

questions.q: NOAA weather broadcasts on a marine VHF radio are on the:
questions.why: Weather radio broadcasts repeat around the clock on the WX channels.

questions.q: On a 100-degree day on the lake, which is a sign of heat exhaustion?
questions.why: Get the person into shade, cool them and give water; confusion or hot dry skin means heat stroke: call 911.

questions.q: The best way to prevent heat illness on a summer sail is to:
options: Drink water early and often, and wear a hat and sunscreen
questions.why: By the time you feel thirsty you are already behind.

questions.q: Where on a lake is the wind usually most patchy and unreliable?
options: In the middle of open water
Close to a high windward shore with trees or buildings
questions.why: Trees and buildings upwind break the breeze into gusts and holes.

questions.q: On a summer afternoon you see a tall cumulus cloud to the west with an anvil top. You should:
options: Head for the dock or reef now
Sail toward it for a better view
questions.why: Anvil tops mean a mature thunderstorm; on this lake they move in quickly from the west.

questions.q: If the lake gets rough and windy, the first sail-handling change on a J/22 is usually to:
options: Reduce power: ease sheets, flatten the sails, reef if you can
questions.why: Depower before the boat is overpowered, not after.

questions.q: A sound-producing device on a small sailboat on the lake is:
questions.why: Boats under 12 metres need some means of making an efficient sound signal.
